bio.en: Amol Avasare is Head of Growth at Anthropic, which grew from $1 billion to over $19 billion in annual recurring revenue in roughly 14 months—one of the fastest growth runs in history.
bio.zh: Amol Avasare 是 Anthropic 的增长负责人，该公司在约 14 个月内将年度经常性收入从 10 亿美元增长到超过 190 亿美元，是史上增长最快的纪录之一。

summary.en: Amol describes the unique challenge of leading growth inside Anthropic, where much past playbook knowledge no longer applies and activation is a core hurdle. He shares clever growth moves like importing memory from ChatGPT and an internal effort called CASH (Claude Accelerate Sustainable Hypergrowth) to automate growth experimentation with Claude. The conversation covers why linear charts have given way to log-linear thinking and how the product's value may be 1000x greater within two years.
summary.zh: Amol 描述了在 Anthropic 领导增长的独特挑战——过去大量的增长方法论不再适用，而激活是核心难题。他分享了诸如“从 ChatGPT 导入记忆”等巧妙的增长动作，以及一个名为 CASH（Claude 加速可持续超增长）的内部项目，用 Claude 自动化增长实验。对话还涵盖为何线性图表已被对数线性思维取代，以及产品价值可能在两年内提升 1000 倍。

turns.zh: 很多公司声称是有史以来增长最快的。Anthropic 真的是。你们 2025 年初 10 亿 ARR。我看到的最后数字是 190 亿 ARR。那是 14 个月从 1 美元到 190 亿美元。

(00:12:13): I think then probably the big differences is I would say that roughly 70% of what I spend my time on is what we internally refer to as success disasters. So if you think about each of those categories on acquisition, on activation, on monetization, there's just a ton of firefighting jumping from one urgent thing to another. And then things like we have a lot of new products coming up like, okay, you ship Cowork, now what? When is the right time that we should lean in as a growth team to start optimizing the core adoption funnel for Cowork? So it's probably 70% just crazy firefighting, 30%, more bread and butter stuff.
turns.zh: 我会说他们不完全错。我们非常非常 lucky 有世界最好模型。我们 lucky 有 Claude Code 和 Cowork 这种产品。它当然让生活容易得多。话说回来我会说这是我人生中最难的工作，那是做过创始人、投行银行家和其他那些，挺难。如果我看我们这里增长团队做什么，我觉得最终是你在正常公司会想的同样类别的东西。我们 care 获客——怎么让更多人进门、进门的人的意图。我们 care 激活——注册流程、funnel 人到对的产品、让他们成功。我们 care 变现——免费到付费转化、定价和打包所有那些类别的工作是一样的。(00:12:13)：我觉得然后大概大不同是我会说我大约 70% 时间花在我们内部叫 success disasters 的。那是事情太好了现在别的在坏。我觉得在快速增长公司工作过的人——你像 Facebook、Uber、DoorDash 早期——viscerally 理解这个，scale 这么多带来很多挑战。所以你想每个那些类别——获客、激活、变现——就有大量 firefighting 从一个紧急跳到另一个。经常极其痛苦。有趣的是你看所有图都绿、全往上右、大家就 emotional 上挺难。所以你得退一步 realize 我们很 lucky 有这些问题。(00:13:07)：但那 70% 时间就是这些 firefighting success disasters。我觉得剩 30% 就是更标准……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. I'm going to dig into a lot of that stuff. One of the cleverest growth moves you all made recently was this idea of importing memory from ChatGPT where you just made it really easy and jumped on this trend of people getting really excited about Anthropic. Is there anything you could share about the behind the scenes story of that feature?
turns.zh: 好。我要 dig into 很多那个。你们最近做的最聪明增长动作之一是从 ChatGPT 导入记忆这个 idea，你让大家很容易、跳上大家对 Anthropic 兴奋的趋势。那个 feature 背后故事有什么能分享？

turns.speaker: Amol Avasare
turns.en: We're just thinking about what can we do to improve the cold start problem and improve the new user experience. I think that activation is a really big challenge in AI. And so that's one example of something that we shipped that was very specific to a moment in time. But ultimately that you zoom out, it's like, okay, how do you really make it easier for people who are signing up to have Claude understand who they are and understand how Claude can help them and get them to the right place?
turns.zh: 我们就在想怎么改进冷启动问题、改进新用户体验。我觉得激活在 AI 是真大挑战。那是一个我们 ship 的、非常特定于一个时间点的东西的例子。但最终你 zoom out 就 okay，你怎么真让注册的人更容易让 Claude 理解他们是谁、理解 Claude 怎么帮他们、把他们带到对的地方？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to follow that thread, activation. That's something that comes up a ton when I talk to people leading, driving growth on AI products. It's just there are so much stuff trying to get your attention these days for people to get to a place where they, okay, wow, this is really going to be something I want to keep using. It proves to be really hard. And it's also just unreliable sometimes, it's not going to be magical. It's AI, it's non-deterministic. I guess, one, is just how important is focusing on activation, getting people to that aha moment with AI products? And two, what are some things you've learned about how to do that well with Claude or AI in general?
turns.zh: 我想跟激活那条线。那是我和领导驱动 AI 产品增长的人聊时大量出现的。就是现在有那么多东西试得到你注意、让人到那个 wow 这真是我要继续用的地方。证明挺难。也有时不可靠、不会 magical。是 AI、非确定。我猜一是聚焦激活多重要、让人到 AI 产品的 aha 时刻？二是什么你学到怎么用 Claude 或 AI 一般做好那个？

turns.speaker: Amol Avasare
turns.en: Yeah, it's a good question. I think that activation, it's critical and defining that as early activation, call it day zero, day one product experience. I think that historically anyone who's been in growth or been in product understands that that's usually one of the highest levers that you have to actually even increase longer term retention. And I think that the importance of that has just gotten exponentially higher. Now, zooming out, I feel like one of the biggest problems in the industry is capability overhang where the models are just getting better so quickly. And the real challenge is on the product side of how do we start to diffuse those benefits to people where even internally, there's new models coming internally and you're sitting there, you're so busy. And when a new model's available, you need to really carve out time to be like, "What can this do? How do I need to update my priors?" (00:16:14): And if you think about more broadly for most people, you may have a model that is like, you may have AGI or some model that can do all sorts of crazy things, but if people's instinct is to come there and be like, "Hey, what's the weather in SF?" Then they're not going to get the most out of the product. And so I think that it's tough because the model capabilities are rising so much. So if I think about, okay, back when we had, I don't know, I want to say Opus 4, there's a series of things the model can do at that point, and Opus 4.5 unlocked a whole bunch of new things. You think about, okay, we sit there, we've got this new model, Opus 4. The time to then go and run a bunch of tests, figure out, okay, there's the capabilities from this new model, what are the right on ramps to guide people to those features? (00:17:03): You run tests, you get the learnings, you then ship a new flow. By then, you may already have the next model, which unlocks newer capabilities that makes all these learnings irrelevant. So it's actually just a really difficult problem to stay on top of. I think that many of the same things, same old trends in growth and activation remain, I think, accurate where to me it's like ultimately some of the highest leverages from finding the right product or the right feature for the right user. And I think that one learning, seeing this time and time again across companies, actually the right friction helps and adding more friction usually works if you do it the right way. I think that's something I've consistently seen that we've seen here as well. So to me, I think it's really being able to identify what are the characteristics of a user that allows you to then recommend them to the right feature or product and not being shy about adding friction to do that, I think is probably the single biggest thing that's important here.
turns.zh: 对，好问题。我觉得激活——定义为早期激活，叫 day zero、day one 产品体验——我觉得历史上在增长或产品的人都理解那通常是你提升长期留存的最高杠杆之一。我觉得那个重要性指数级更高了。现在 zooming out，我觉得行业最大问题之一是能力 overhang，模型变得更好太快。真挑战在产品侧怎么开始把那些 benefit 扩散给人，甚至内部新模型来、你坐着那么忙。新模型可用时你真得 carve out 时间 like 这能做什么？我怎么更新我的 priors？(00:16:14)：如果你想更广对大多数人，你可能有模型能做各种疯狂事，但如果人的 instinct 是来那里 like 嘿 SF 天气怎样？那他们不会从产品得到最多。所以我觉得难因为模型能力上升那么多。所以如果我想，好，回我们有 Opus 4 时有一系列模型能做的事，Opus 4.5 解锁了一堆新事。你想 okay 我们坐这有新模型 Opus 4。到 then 去跑一堆测试、figure out 好有新模型能力、什么是引导人到那些 feature 的对 on ramp？(00:17:03)：你跑测试、得 learning、ship 新流程。到 then 你可能已有下一个模型解锁新能力让这些 learning 无关。所以它就是个真难的保持……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: When I asked Ben Mann, one of the co-founders, former podcast guest, what to ask you about, and this is what he highlighted, is your experience, especially at Mercury redoing onboarding and making it magical. And basically he's in the same place as you of just how important it is for people to understand what the AI tool is capable of to help people decide to use it and stick with it. Is there an example of something you changed in onboarding that helped significantly improve activation?
turns.zh: 我问 Ben Mann——联合创始人、前播客嘉宾——该问你什么，他 highlight 的就是这个，你的经验尤其在 Mercury 重做 onboarding 让它 magical。基本他在同一位置，怎么重要让人理解 AI 工具能做什么、帮人决定用它、坚持。有没有例子你在 onboarding 改了什么显著提升激活？

turns.speaker: Amol Avasare
turns.en: Yeah, it's a great question. And I like that it brings up Mercury. I talk about their product a lot. So worked on the growth team at Mercury, I think it's a fantastic product. It's something many people use, and the reason they use it is because the better banking experience than its-
turns.zh: 对，好问题。我喜欢它 bring up Mercury。我常谈他们产品。在 Mercury 增长团队工作，我觉得是 fantastic 产品。很多人用，原因是比其……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I'm a very happy customer just to put that out there. I love it.
turns.zh: 对，我是非常开心客户就说一下。我爱它。

turns.speaker: Amol Avasare
turns.en: It's a great product. Highly recommend it. They have personal banking. Everyone should go and use it.
turns.zh: 好产品。强烈推荐。他们有个人银行。大家都该去用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Right. They just launched that.
turns.zh: 对。他们刚 launch 那个。

turns.speaker: Amol Avasare
turns.en: And so I think that the interesting thing about Mercury is the core value is that it's a better experience. That's the reason you use it. You're not getting better other things, just it's a better product experience. And so that ethos is very, very deeply held within the company. It comes from a number of the founders. And I think that we had a big push one quarter when I was there on the onboarding flow. So onboarding flows for banking institutions and regulated entities are extremely complex. The amount of time I've spent on the difference between a registered agent address and a legal address and a physical address, these things are very, very complex. And we basically looked at the onboarding flow and we were like, okay, we've invested so much in quality and the rest of the product, but we haven't really done it here. And this is the first experience that people have. (00:19:48): And so we said, forget metrics, forget growth, forget everything else. As the growth team on conversion, we're going to spend a whole quarter fixing quality in this flow. And so that's all we did. Forget the metrics. We're just going to make this as good of an experience as we can and fix all these. You go back from one field to the other field and adding in your beneficial ownership details. And it actually ended up being, and probably until I joined here, the single most impactful quarter that I've ever had as a growth PM in terms of the impact that it had. And so we saw a significant uplift on basically our onboarding started to completion from just focusing on quality. (00:20:28): And so that to me is a broader learning around quality drives growth that I think I've tried to bring to Anthropic. I think for us at Anthropic, some of the things that we've done in the onboarding flow is basically we ask users questions around who they are, what their interest areas are. And we then use that to recommend different products and features. And number of people look at the flow and they're like, "You have so much friction. It's such a long flow." And I'm like, "We have the data. We're kind of happy with how that's performing."
turns.zh: 所以我觉得 Mercury 有趣的是核心价值是更好体验。那是你用的原因。你不会得到更好的别的，就是更好产品体验。那个 ethos 在公司非常深深持有。来自一些创始人。我觉得我在那里时有一季度大推 onboarding 流程。银行机构和受监管实体的 onboarding 流程极复杂。我花在注册代理地址 vs 法定地址 vs 物理地址区别上的时间，这些东西非常复杂。我们基本看 onboarding 流程就好我们投了那么多在质量和产品其余部分但这里没真做。这是人的第一体验。(00:19:48)：所以我们说忘指标、忘增长、忘一切。作为转化增长团队我们要花一整季度修这个流程的质量。就做那个。忘指标。就让它尽可能好的体验、修所有这些。你从一个字段回另一个字段、加 beneficial ownership 详情。它其实 turn out 是、可能直到我来这里、我作为增长 PM 有过的单季度最大影响。我们看到 onboarding 开始到完成显著提升就因为聚焦质量。(00:20:28)：所以那对我来说是更广的学习：质量驱动增长，我觉得我试带到 Anthropic。我觉得我们在 Anthropic onboarding 流程做的一些是基本问用户问题关于他们是谁、兴趣领域。然后我们用那个推荐不同产品和 feature。很多人看流程 like……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is your kind of philosophy on good friction versus bad friction?
turns.zh: 你对好摩擦 vs 坏摩擦的哲学是什么？

turns.speaker: Amol Avasare
turns.en: I've just seen time and time again at every job I've been in growth that adding friction and adding the right steps leads to higher conversion and higher funnel completion. So you want to get rid of... And especially if you have high volume, you should test the majority of this and just learn and see, does this apply to your business as well? But you want to get rid of annoying friction that doesn't add value. But I think the most simple understanding people have is just solve time for value, cut all the steps and just get them into the product. And that doesn't work most times. I think if you've really thoroughly tested your flows, I look at the companies I've been at, MasterClass. If you go through MasterClass's purchase flow right now, you'll go through all these steps in this quiz when you land on, when you're trying to buy. (00:21:57): And you're like, "I came here to buy and it's taking me through all these questions, what are you here for, et cetera." I think it's easy to look at that and be like, "Why do they have this? This is a terrible thing. Just cut it all." And it's like, no, that's been thoroughly tested. And actually that was a significant revenue driver because it helps users feel that the product is for them by understanding what their interests are and then recommending the content and classes there. One of the growth PMs on our team left to join Calm, Calm.com, the meditation app. If you go to Calm's, their landing page and you go through their purchase flow, their login flow, you'll see a quiz. It's not a coincidence that at Mercury we also tested, I think Immad posted on Twitter, we broke out some steps in onboarding. And just having one screen, if you have five or six different form inputs and you often break that into two screens and reduce the cognitive load to people, that is something that performs well. (00:22:54): We added steps into the flow there that actually performed well, same at Anthropic. So I think that the takeaway to me is cut friction when it doesn't add to the experience of helping a user understand why the product is for them. But if you can help users understand a product, why product is for them and how to use it and what's most relevant to them, and it's going to add friction, don't shy away from it. Test it, confirm that it works for you, but I think this is something that most growth practitioners deeply understand.
turns.zh: 我在每个增长工作里一次次看到加摩擦和加对步骤导致更高转化和更高漏斗完成。所以你想去掉……尤其如果你有高量你该测大部分这个就学、看这适用于你业务吗？但你想去掉不增值的烦人摩擦。但我觉得最简单的理解是就解决 time to value、cut 所有步骤就把他们弄进产品。那大多时候不 work。我觉得如果你真彻底测过流程，我看我待过的公司，MasterClass。如果你现在过 MasterClass 购买流程，你会过这些 quiz 步骤当你着陆、试买时。(00:21:57)：你就我来买还带我过这些问题、你来这为什么等等。我觉得容易看那个 like 为什么有这个？这是 terrible。就全 cut。而 no 那被彻底测过。其实那是显著收入驱动因为它帮用户感觉产品是给他们的、通过理解他们兴趣然后推荐内容和课程。我们团队一个增长 PM 离开去 Calm、Calm.com 冥想 app。如果你去 Calm 着陆页过购买流程、登录流程你会看到 quiz。不是巧合在 Mercury 我们也测过，Immad 发过 Twitter，我们在 onboarding 拆出步骤。就一个屏幕如果你有五六个不同表单输入你常 break 成两屏减少认知负荷，那个 perform 好。(00:22:54)：我们在那里加步骤 perform 好，Anthropic 同样。所以我觉得 takeaway 是 cut……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And for them is really important there, what you described is adding friction to better understand who they are so that you know how to recommend the right thing for them.
turns.zh: 对他们在那里很重要，你描述的是加摩擦更好理解他们是谁这样你知道怎么推荐对的东西。

turns.speaker: Amol Avasare
turns.en: Correct. Yes. And that done right, it just flows through. So it helps you with activation, but then it helps you with lifecycle. You know more about those users and why they're here. And most sophisticated businesses, you can then, even if someone drops off, you can do lookalike targeting and you can get them at the ad layer as well. So that initial piece of how you understand who the user is just like it's a juice that just keeps on giving if you then use it right for the down funnel.
turns.zh: 对。是。那个做好就 flow through。所以帮你激活、然后帮你 lifecycle。你更了解那些用户和为什么来。大多数成熟业务你能然后即使有人 drop off 你能做 lookalike targeting、在广告层获取他们。所以最初你理解用户是谁那块就像果汁不断给如果你下游用对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Everyone's about to go do a bunch of tear downs of Claude's onboarding, MasterClass onboarding, Mercury onboarding. As a tangent, I was at this PM dinner recently and I was asking all the PMs, how has your role as a PM changed most with AI? Where has AI most impacted what you do? And one of the PM's answer that is actually doing competitive analysis, doing a bunch of teardowns of what other people are doing for pricing pages and onboarding. So it's easy to do now. Just, "Hey, Cowork..." I don't know, would you use Cowork for this or Claude? What would you use for that? Okay, this is good. Help people pick which tool to use. If you want to go do a bunch of teardowns of other competitors' onboarding flows, what would you use?
turns.zh: 大家要去拆解 Claude onboarding、MasterClass onboarding、Mercury onboarding。作为 tangent 我最近在这个 PM 晚宴问所有 PM：AI 怎么最改变你 PM 角色？AI 最影响你做什么？一个 PM 回答其实是做竞品分析、拆解别人定价页和 onboarding。现在容易做。就嘿 Cowork……不知道你会用 Cowork 做这个还是 Claude？你会用什么？好，帮大家选哪个工具。如果你想拆解竞品 onboarding 流程你会用什么？

turns.speaker: Amol Avasare
turns.en: You can use Cowork for this, right? So you have Cowork with the Chrome extension. So if you task Cowork with a Chrome extension, go and look for these flows and give me a view of what's working, what's not. That's definitely something that Cowork can do.
turns.zh: 你能用 Cowork 做这个对吧？Cowork 有 Chrome 扩展。如果你 task Cowork 带 Chrome 扩展去看这些流程、给我什么 work 什么不的 view。那是 Cowork 能做的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Cool. And I imagine that's one of the challenges is you have all these tools now, just which ones for me. By the way, the Chrome extension, I use it all the time. It's amazing. I want to drill a little bit further into the growth org. There's this whole meme on Twitter the other day of just like you have one growth marketer driving all growth at Anthropic and it's like, okay, that's crazy. How many growth people are there? What's the rough org structure of the growth team?
turns.zh: 酷。我猜挑战之一是你有所有这些工具就哪个给我。顺便 Chrome 扩展我一直用。太棒了。我想再 drill 增长组织。Twitter 上有个 meme 就像你们只有一个增长 marketer 驱动 Anthropic 所有增长就 okay 那 crazy。有多少增长人？增长团队大致 org 结构？

turns.speaker: Amol Avasare
turns.en: We're roughly maybe 40 people now. And so we are, I think, structured very much like a traditional growth team in that we have horizontals of growth platform and monetization who think about the sphere of growth across the entirety of our products. And then we have more audience-focused growth pods. You can think about B2B growth, you can think about Claude Code growth, knowledge worker growth, API growth. So really these audiences to keep a narrow focus, which is the thing you have to do when you have so many different products. And then these horizontals that think about things across the board.
turns.zh: 我们现在大约 40 人。我们我觉得结构非常像传统增长团队，有 horizontals of growth platform 和 monetization 想跨所有产品的增长 sphere。然后有更受众聚焦的增长 pod。你能想 B2B 增长、Claude Code 增长、知识工作者增长、API 增长。真这些受众保持窄聚焦，当你有这么多产品你该做的。然后那些 horizontals 跨一切想。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And is it across a team of engineers, designers, PMs? What's the functions within this growth org?
turns.zh: 是跨团队工程师、设计师、PM 吗？增长 org 内什么职能？

turns.speaker: Amol Avasare
turns.en: Yeah, it's engineers, designers, PMs, data. I think that overall the shape of the org is quite similar to, I'd say a traditional growth team. Probably the things that are maybe different is that I think that we index a lot more towards larger swings as opposed to smaller optimizations. If I think about a traditional growth team, I would've probably done maybe 60%, 70% of my time on small to medium bets, 20% to 30% on larger swings. And I think that for us, we flip it a lot. We do much more the other way where it's 70-30 or more like 50-50 rather than indexing towards smaller bets. That's probably one of the biggest changes, I think.
turns.zh: 对，工程师、设计师、PM、数据。我觉得 org shape 整体和传统增长团队挺像。大概不同是我们 index 更多大 swing vs 小优化。如果我想传统增长团队大概 60%、70% 时间在小到中 bet、20% 到 30% 大 swing。我觉得我们 flip 很多。我们做更多另一边 70-30 或更像 50-50 vs index 小 bet。那大概最大变化之一。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just to highlight that, what's interesting there is at the scale you guys are at, a 1% win is massive in the scheme of things. So it's interesting that even at the scale you're at, you're not focusing on these micro optimizations.
turns.zh: 就 highlight 那个，有趣的是在你们规模 1% win 在 scheme 里 massive。所以有趣即使你规模你也不聚焦这些微优化。

turns.speaker: Amol Avasare
turns.en: It is easy. You could easily focus on these small optimizations and then you tally them up at the end of the quarter and you're like, "Look how much impact we made." And you could do that.
turns.zh: 容易。你能容易聚焦这些小优化然后季度末 tally 就看我们做了多少影响。你能那样做。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Another billion. No big deal.
turns.zh: 又一个十亿。没什么。

turns.speaker: Amol Avasare
turns.en: Yeah. But the thing is we've been tracking at 10X year-on-year, and that's the thing that we keep in mind. And I think it ultimately comes down to our fixation of this company about the exponential. I think if you look at anyone who's talking from Anthropic about basically anything, we always talk about the exponential. It's effectively as model capabilities continue to grow on an exponential and the tools around them enable a better job of diffusing that into useful use cases, you basically just keep unlocking new markets where the value of those markets significantly dwarfs what the value of the previous markets were. And agentic coding's a great example. It didn't exist a year, a year and a half ago. And then now just the value of agentic coding is bigger than the previous market of AI coding use. (00:28:22): And so I think that is the core thing here where just that the future product value is in order of magnitude higher than it is today. And I think about, I don't know, a normal business, number of companies that I maybe mentioned, or you think about a trading app or a grocery delivery product, many of the leading companies, they're great businesses. But if I think about what is the product value that a company, like a standard, call it a grocery delivery app, what is the product value you get as an end user today versus two years from now? I look at it as like, okay, in two years from now, even if you're shipping all these new products, as an end user, the value you get-
turns.zh: 对。但我们一直 10 倍年同比、那是我们记住的。我觉得最终归到我们公司对指数的 fixation。如果你看 Anthropic 任何人谈基本上任何事我们总谈指数。effectively 随模型能力继续指数增长、周围工具 enable 更好 diffusion 到有用用例你基本持续解锁新市场，那些市场价值显著 dwarf 前市场。agentic coding 是好例子。一年一年半前不存在。然后现在 agentic coding 价值比之前 AI coding 用市场大。(00:28:22)：所以我觉得那是核心这里，未来产品价值比今天高一个量级。我想 normal business，我提到的公司数，或你想交易 app 或杂货配送产品，很多领先公司是好业务。但如果我想一个公司比如标准杂货配送 app 的产品价值，你作为终端用户今天 vs 两年后？我看 like 两年后即使你 ship 所有这些新产品，作为终端用户你得到的价值……

turns.speaker: Amol Avasare
turns.en: You're shipping all these new products. As an end user, the value you get from that product maybe goes up 30 to 50% if the company's done a really good job of shipping new features. It's not exponential though. (00:29:12): And so if I think about, "Okay, you're here today. In two years, you're going to have 30 to 50% more product value." Then as a growth team, the relative differential of the product value in two years from now relative to today, I can actually capture a decent percentage of that with the small to medium optimizations that typically have higher conviction as opposed to larger bets. (00:29:36): But for Anthropic, it's not really that way, where because of the exponential and our products being very, very, very ... The product value coming from AI, the product value that we will deliver in two years' time is probably a 1,000x, a 100 to a 1,000x what it is today. (00:29:58): And so if I think about that, and it's like there's so much value on offer, you need to shift more towards, "Okay, we need to take larger bets and we need to not miss the forest for the trees." And so that's why we still do all the smaller optimizations. It really matters, and no one else is going to do some of these things and so we need to do it. The compounding value is not immaterial, but we do take on much larger core productey type of swings as well. (00:30:25): So you mentioned the Chrome Extension. That is now the thing that underpins a number of use cases on Cowork and Claude Code as well. And that's something that the growth team built. That's a very AI-peeled product that is a very research-heavy product that we were just bullish on it. We had an engineer who was very bullish on it and we were just like, "Hey, no one else is doing it. We're going to do it." And so that's the sort of thing that I wouldn't have done at another company.
turns.zh: 你 ship 所有这些新产品。作为终端用户你从那个产品得到的价值大概涨 30 到 50% 如果公司在 ship 新 feature 上做得很好。不是指数。(00:29:12)：所以如果我想好你今天在这、两年后你会有 30 到 50% 更多产品价值。那作为增长团队，两年后产品价值相对今天的相对差异，我其实能用小到中优化 capture 那个的 decent 百分比，那些通常有更高 conviction vs 大 bet。(00:29:36)：但对 Anthropic 不是那样，因为指数和我们产品非常非常非常……来自 AI 的产品价值，我们两年后交付的产品价值大概是 1000 倍、100 到 1000 倍今天。(00:29:58)：所以如果我想那个就那里有那么多价值 offer 你得 shift 更多到好我们得 take 更大 bet、我们得不见森林只见树。所以那就是为什么我们仍做所有小优化。真 matter、没人会做这些事所以得做。复合价值不 immaterial 但我们确实也 take 更大核心产品类 swing。(00:30:25)：所以你提到 Chrome 扩展。那个现在 underpin 很多 Cowork 和 Claude Code 用例。那是增长团队建的。那是非常 AI pilled 产品、非常研究重的产品我们就 bullish。我们有个工程师很 bullish 就好没人做、我们做。那是我在别的公司不会做的事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, wow. I did not know that. So one takeaway here is there's stuff to extract from your advice that is only true in Anthropic and then there's, what can other companies learn from this experience that you've had? (00:31:09): So one is, is your sense that if you're working in AI, shift more of the pie chart towards bigger bets because in the future, the opportunity is so large, you want to find those as soon as possible versus micro-optimize?
turns.zh: 哦哇。我不知道那个。所以一个 takeaway 是从你建议里有只对 Anthropic true 的、别的公司能从你经验学到什么？(00:31:09)：所以一是你感觉如果你在 AI 工作，把饼图更多 shift 到大 bet 因为未来机会那么大你想尽快找那些 vs 微优化？

turns.speaker: Amol Avasare
turns.en: To be more specific there, I would say that if the primary value that your product delivers is underpinned by AI as a central element of it, then I think you should operate this way. So I don't know, companies like Lovable, Cursor, all these great businesses that are, as the exponential rises, their value props are also going to continue to rise significantly. (00:31:50): If you're building a product where it's an AI-first product, then I would definitely operate in this way. I think if you're building a product where it's not necessarily an AI- first product and you have some AI features that are on the side, but it's not the core of your value, I don't know that I would operate this way. It would depend on how is the rest of the product org staffed and how is the growth org staffed in relation to that.
turns.zh: 更具体说，我会说如果你产品交付的核心价值以 AI 为核心要素 underpin，我觉得你该这样 operate。我不知道，像 Lovable、Cursor 这些好业务，随指数上升它们 value prop 也会继续显著上升。(00:31:50)：如果你在建 AI-first 产品我 definitely 这样 operate。如果你建的不一定是 AI-first、有一些 AI feature 在旁边但不是核心价值，我不知道我会这样 operate。取决于产品 org 怎么 staff 和增长 org 怎么 relation 那个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, awesome. And then in terms of the way you are structured, I thought that was really interesting. It's a combination of different sorts of things. So there's the API growth, there's Claude Code growth, but then there's also personas, like a vertical of knowledge workers and B2B. Is that intentional, some specific bets and one just broad market opportunity?
turns.zh: 好，太好了。然后你们结构方式我觉得很有趣。是不同种类组合。有 API 增长、Claude Code 增长但也有人设如知识工作者和 B2B 纵向。那是 intentional 吗，特定 bet 和一个 broad 市场机会？

turns.speaker: Amol Avasare
turns.en: When you have one product, it's easier to have a growth team that's more purely on the funnel. It's like you have the conversion, you have activation, you have monetization. But as you start to get into having multiple products, I think that's harder because if you do that, then if you just have one activation team, for example, but then you have Claude Code, you have Cowork, you have all the other things. They're very different audiences and they're very different sets of cross-functional stakeholders internally. (00:33:01): So we're kind of looking at, what is the thing? And all org structures are not perfect and they're right for a point in time, but we're looking for what is the structure that allows us to have as much focus. Focus is a really big thing, and on audience and problems. (00:33:19): And also, the tie-ins to cross-functional partners is really, really important. The folks on our Claude Code growth team, they work extremely closely with Cat and Boris and the others on that team. And so that tie-in is really important as well.
turns.zh: 当你有一个产品更容易有增长团队更纯在 funnel。你有转化、激活、变现。但当你开始有多个产品我觉得那更难因为如果你就一个激活团队但你又有 Claude Code、Cowork、所有别的。它们是非常不同受众和非常不同跨职能 stakeholder 内部。(00:33:01)：所以我们在看什么是 thing？所有 org 结构不完美、它们对某时间点对。但我们在找什么结构让我们有尽可能多聚焦。聚焦是很大的事，在受众和问题上。(00:33:19)：还有和跨职能 partner 的 tie-in 非常非常重要。我们 Claude Code 增长团队的人和 Cat 和 Boris 和那个团队其他人 work 非常紧密。那个 tie-in 也重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So you've done growth at a lot of different companies, a lot of basically, let's call it traditional growth before Anthropic. How else is growth as a function and as a skillset changing with the rise of AI, AI products, and AI startups?
turns.zh: 你在很多不同公司做过增长，基本叫传统增长 before Anthropic。增长作为职能和技能集随 AI、AI 产品、AI 创业公司崛起还在怎么变？

turns.speaker: Amol Avasare
turns.en: I think if your core product value is very backed by AI, then it is shifting where you're skewing more towards larger bets as opposed to smaller, medium experiments. I think in other things, it may be a big thing related to this that I think will accelerate this, which I am really interested to see how it will play out, is we are starting to look at how do we automate growth, which I think is a really interesting area. (00:34:16): So our growth platform team, we're very lucky we have Alexey Komissarouk who teaches growth engineering at Reforge, and he's just the guy on the team. And so he is driving this effort. The name is, it's a little cringey. I didn't come up with it. And it's called CASH, which is Claude Accelerates Sustainable Hypergrowth. I did not come up with that, but really it's an effort to look at how can we use Claude to automate growth experimentation? (00:34:48): And it is still very, very small. It's still very, very early. We kicked it off only, I think, a couple of months ago. I think before Opus 4.5, it wasn't really possible. We were just not seeing the results. And more recently with Opus 4.6 we're like, "Okay, this is headed in the right direction." (00:35:07): And so this, I think, it will happen more and more across the industry, where basically if you think about, okay ... I think this can happen all across product, but growth teams in particular because there's this whole body of work that is very small optimizations, I think are just more inherently suited to tackle this earlier. (00:35:29): I think if you think about the lifecycle of shipping, there's four parts to it. One is identifying opportunities. How good is Claude at actually identifying opportunities based on different trends, based on previous trends that Claude has seen in the past? Second is then building the actual feature and getting it ready to ship. Third is testing and ensuring that it meets your quality bar and your brand bar. And then fourth is then once you've actually shipped the thing, analyzing the data, gathering the learnings. (00:36:02): If you think about that as the loop of, "Okay, these are four things that you can eval and hill climb on each of these areas and understand how good is a model doing for you there." And we basically think about it in that four ways and we are scoring how good is Claude doing in each of those areas. (00:36:24): And so we've been testing this at pretty small scale right now. It's been a lot of copy changes and some very minor UI tweaks. It's delivering results and it's like you can push it, press play with it. And it ultimately prints money where I'd say that the win rate is like, I would expect a senior PM to do better. I would say this is a junior PM, two, three years in. I would say this is the win rate that I would expect from a junior PM, but it's not quite at the senior PM level. Although, I think you look at the exponential, this wasn't available at all a couple of months ago. So it's getting better rapidly. (00:37:03): And I think that it's going to change where you'll be able to do this for larger and larger types of experiments. But then you think about the largest types of experiments, I think that I mentioned the four pieces around identifying opportunities, building, testing and shipping. The one I didn't mention there, Lenny, is cross-functional stakeholder management.
turns.zh: 我觉得如果你核心产品价值很 AI backed 那它在 shift 你 skew 更大 bet vs 小中实验。我觉得别的可能和这个相关、我觉得会加速这个的，是我很有兴趣看怎么 play out 的，是我们开始看怎么自动化增长，我觉得是很有趣领域。(00:34:16)：我们增长平台团队，很 lucky 有 Alexey Komissarouk 在 Reforge 教增长工程，他就是那个人。他 driving 这个 effort。名字有点 cringey。不是我起的。叫 CASH——Claude Accelerates Sustainable Hypergrowth。不是我起但真的是看怎么用 Claude 自动化增长实验的 effort。(00:34:48)：仍非常非常小。仍非常非常早。我们几个月前才 kick off。我觉得 Opus 4.5 之前不真可能。我们就没看到结果。最近 Opus 4.6 我们就好这个朝对方向。(00:35:07)：所以这个我觉得会跨行业越来越多发生，基本如果你想 okay……我觉得这能跨产品发生但增长团队尤其因为有这整个非常小优化的工作体我觉得更 inherent 适合更早 tackle 这个。(00:35:29)：如果你想 shipping 生命周期有四部分。一是识别机会。Claude 多擅长基于不同趋势、基于 Claude 过去见过的趋势识别机会？二是然后建实际 feature 准备 ship。三是测试确保达到质量和品牌 bar。然后四是然后一旦你 actual……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's still a need for human brains. There is.
turns.zh: 仍需要人脑。是。

turns.speaker: Amol Avasare
turns.en: And I think that that one is going to mean that in my eyes, the work of PMs is not going away actually, anytime soon. And that piece, especially for larger projects. Usually, you don't need to do as much of it for smaller stuff. You can skip it. But for larger stuff, that piece is not going away.
turns.zh: 我觉得那个在我眼里意味着 PM 的工作其实不 anytime soon 消失。那块尤其对大项目。通常小的不需要那么多。能 skip。但大项目那块不消失。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Until the other stakeholders have their own little agents running around.
turns.zh: 直到其他 stakeholder 有自己的小 agent 跑来跑去。

turns.speaker: Amol Avasare
turns.en: I think that's right. I think that would be the point where it changes. It's funny, we had a difficult meeting a couple of weeks ago, and me and our head of design, Joel, we were debriefing afterwards. And he pings me, he's just like, "Amol, we will have AGI and it will still be impossible to get six people in a room to get to align." And I'm like, "Yeah, I think I can say that."
turns.zh: 我觉得对。我觉得那是改变的点。有趣我们几周前有个难会议，我和我们设计负责人 Joel 之后 debrief。他 ping 我就 Amol 我们会有 AGI 但仍不可能让六个人在房间对齐。我就对我觉得我能说那个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's the harder alignment problem? Oh, okay. This is so interesting and this is exactly where I feel like things are going. So just to be clear what you shared here, there's basically this tool that comes up with experiments to run, to help grow Claude and all the tools. (00:38:36): So it comes up with idea, somebody looks at them, approves, "Cool, let's do these things." Builds it, ships it, tests the results, see how it's doing, and then comes back of, "Here's things that are working." Is that roughly right?
turns.zh: 什么对齐问题更难？好这个太有趣这正是我感觉事往哪走。所以澄清你分享的基本有这个工具出实验 idea 帮 Claude 和所有工具增长。(00:38:36)：所以它出 idea，人看、approve、酷做这些。建、ship、测结果、看怎样、然后回来这是 work 的。大致对吧？

turns.speaker: Amol Avasare
turns.en: It's roughly right. And right now, we have human in the loop approving, but the amount of time, I kind of think about scale in this way of just week on week, are things getting better in each of the areas? Are people spending less time on each of the areas? Are the results getting better in each of the areas? (00:39:04): And as long as week on week, that's getting better, then you're like, "Okay, this whole initiative is scaling." And so that's roughly right, but you can think about it as, I think a lot of this can be automated where human review is not needed. (00:39:17): So we care a lot about our brand, right? So that is something that we do look at right now. We don't want to be shipping something that goes against the brand, but then you can have a skill that contains your brand guidelines and very clear, yet dos and don'ts on brand. (00:39:36): And so all of these types of accompaniments, I think are going to get better. The model's going to get better at understanding how to use them. And so over time, I think that the need to human review this really, really decreases significantly.
turns.zh: 大致对。现在我们有 human in the loop approve，但多少时间我这样想 scale——每周每个领域在变好吗？人在每个领域花更少时间吗？每个领域结果在变好吗？(00:39:04)：只要每周在变好你就好这个 initiative 在 scale。所以大致对，但你能想很多这个能自动化不需要人 review。(00:39:17)：我们很 care 品牌。那是我们现在确实看的。我们不想 ship 违背品牌的东西，但你能有 skill 包含你品牌指南和非常清晰的品牌 dos and don'ts。(00:39:36)：所以所有这些类型的 accompaniment 我觉得会变好。模型会变好理解怎么用它们。所以随时间我觉得需要人 review 这个真显著减少。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, and you could always unship it if it's like, "Oh yeah, that was actually not a great idea." And that's such a good point that we think we need people to do these things forever. And it turns out, "Okay, a skill could do this really well. Here's our brand guidelines, here's our vision, here's our mission, here's our goals, here's what matters to us. Okay, no, let's not ship that thing." (00:40:06): So the reason I think this is so interesting, I've just been watching the expansion of AI doing more of the product development process, in this case the growth process of just, okay, it went from helping you write code, to writing all your code, to reviewing your code. Now it feels like, what are the two ends around this? It's kind of going from the middle up. The top of that is coming up with what to do and then there's the alignment stuff's still very hard. (00:40:32): And then on the other end, it's reviewing the code and then shipping it and then get distribution. That's a whole other thing I want to talk to you about. So what I'm hearing here, and this is exactly what I thought was going to start happening, is AI is now getting really good at telling us what to do, not just taking our orders and building it. (00:40:49): And it feels like the growth version of this is where it starts because it's so much simpler, not that growth is easy, but just like it's data-driven, there's this loop that you talk about. So I think this is such an interesting sign of things to come across just generally, product.
turns.zh: 对你总能 unship 如果 like 哦那其实不是好 idea。这很好一点我们想我们需要人永远做这些。turns out 好一个 skill 能做这个很好。这是品牌指南、愿景、使命、目标、什么对我们重要。好不 ship 那个。(00:40:06)：所以我觉得这个太有趣的原因是我一直在看 AI 做更多产品开发过程的扩张，这次是增长过程就 okay，它从帮你写代码到写所有代码到 review 你代码。现在感觉这个两端是什么？从中间往上。上面是想出做什么然后对齐仍很难。(00:40:32)：然后另一端是 review 代码然后 ship 然后得分发。那是另一件事我想和你谈。所以我听到这个——正是我以为会开始发生的——AI 现在变得很擅长告诉我们做什么，不只接我们订单建它。(00:40:49)：感觉增长版这是开始的地方因为它更简单，不是说增长容易但就 data-driven、有你谈的 loop。所以我觉得这是 across 产品 generally 未来的信号。

turns.speaker: Amol Avasare
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just putting that out there. Okay. So something that I'm constantly thinking about along these lines is just the future of product PM engineering, how those roles shift over time based on the stuff we're talking about. (00:41:18): How are you working together as a triad and where do you see these roles going? What's most going to change, do you think, across these three roles?
turns.zh: 就放那。好。我一直在想这条线就是产品 PM 工程的未来，这些角色怎么随时间 shift 基于我们聊的。(00:41:18)：你怎么作为 triad work？你觉得这些角色去哪？三个角色什么最会变？

turns.speaker: Amol Avasare
turns.en: This is something that we talk about and think about frequently, and the picture changes rapidly. So sometimes when things break, execution, like the bottlenecks break, historically in the past it's like, "Okay, now you need to hire more engineers, you need to hire more designers," et cetera. And it's more just a lifecycle thing of, where is the lifecycle of your team and that specific pod to identify where the bottleneck is? (00:41:51): But now when things break, you need to still look at it, of, "Okay, is it the actual ratio or is there also underlying technological shifts that are also causing this to break?" And so that's an interesting thing. I think that smaller companies, if I'm at a 15 or 20-person company, I'm the only PM there working with some designers and engineers, I think in the smaller companies, you'll see probably the biggest blend, where the PM will be doing all sorts of ... They'll be designing, shipping, et cetera, and I think you just have extreme bifurcation. (00:42:24): You know, at larger organizations, more scaled organizations, I think the jury is still very much out. You speak to people even internally here, and different people and different teams will have different views of, "Okay, how much are these roles coming together versus how much are these roles going to be separate?" I think that it's not to say even the PMs, number of PMs are shipping, and themselves shipping and pushing PRs, et cetera. (00:42:51): But if I look at, okay, across what I'm seeing, I think that it's clear that while PMs and designers are getting more leverage from AI, engineering is getting the most leverage right now. I look at tools like Claude Code, and the amount of leverage engineers are getting from them is higher than, I think the leverage that designers and PMs are getting from them today. (00:43:15): Now, this is rapidly also changing, but that to me is my view today. And so if you think about, okay, a default team, which is, say five engineers, one designer, one PM. With Claude Code, that five engineers is two to 3xed. And the PMs and designers have also increased, but now they're managing what is effectively a much larger group of engineers. (00:43:42): And so even though the headcount and the org structure hasn't changed, you're now just dealing with a situation of maybe 15 to 20 engineers in the old world, one and a half to two PMs, and maybe one and a half to two designers. And so we're seeing that that's putting a lot of strain on PM and design. And it's not everywhere. (00:44:04): I look at teams like Claude Code and I think that, or because that product is so technical, it's probably just the right thing, where the PMs are all basically engineers themselves anyway. But we had a product, like a PM lead on site the other week, and we were all just talking about this where across the board we're feeling this, where PM and design is just squeezed. It's just absolutely squeezed. (00:44:26): And we're like, "Is the right thing here, we just need to actually hire a ton more PMs?" And it could actually be where we land. On growth, how I think about it is, one, we are hiring a number of growth PMs. We desperately need people who are very, very good, and we are hiring. turns.en: Yeah. I think three things that come to mind there. First is I go back to something I said earlier, which is that we very much think about things from an exponential lens. And if you are thinking about things from a linear lens, you'll see the world very, very differently, right, because you look at where we are today and you're like, "Okay, but how much better can it be in two, three years?" I think if you're looking at it from an exponential lens and you understand how exponentials work, then you just realize that a lot of this stuff is actually going to be happening sooner than people think if you're looking at it from a linear lens. And then if you understand that there could be upsides and downsides and the range of outcomes here, I think we very much need to be talking about the downsides so we can avoid them and push towards the upsides. (01:33:36): I think most people at the company are optimists. We're very optimistic about the future. I think it's just we understand the risk is like it is not a guaranteed that we end up in a good place. And not enough people are talking about the risks, I think, in productive ways and who have the know-how of the risks. I think there's people who may talk about the risks but are not in the game. And so they don't actually know fully. They're not surgical on what the specific risks are, but we're in the game, we understand what's happening. And so that's one piece. I think the second is, I think, we actually believe in this stuff more strongly than we say externally. So it is just such a key part of how we think internally that sometimes we just reword your statements because it's like people might just think we're being too over the top, but internally, that's how we think, and what we're putting out is a softer version of that at times. (01:34:28): And then I think the third piece is going to what Ben said where we think a lot about driving the race to the top. And so it's like if you're not in the game and you're shouting from the sidelines, no one cares. It's just the reality of how the world works. No one really cares. If you're in the game and you're a leading player and what you're doing is working, you can influence people who are also in the game to take the right actions. And so that is the core of it. If we just pack up and go home, you have no influence on this thing. And if you stay in the game and you're like, commercially, you're doing great, and then you have ways to influence that, okay, these are the principles and put that into the conversation and make more people sort of believe in those things.
turns.zh: 对。我觉得三件事 come to mind。第一回到我之前说的我们非常从指数 lens 想事。如果你从线性 lens 想你会非常不同看世界，因为你看今天在哪就 okay 但两三年能多好？我觉得如果你从指数 lens 看、理解指数怎么 work 你就 realize 很多这个其实比大家想更早发生如果你从线性 lens 看。然后如果你理解可能有 upside 和 downside、outcome range 我觉得我们非常需要谈 downside 这样我们能避免、push towards upside。(01:33:36)：我觉得公司大多数人乐观。我们对未来非常乐观。我觉得就我们理解风险是不 guaranteed 我们到好地方。不够多人 productive 地谈风险、有 know-how 的。我觉得有人谈风险但不在 game。所以他们不真知道。他们不 surgical 在具体风险什么。但我们在 game、我们理解什么在发生。所以那是一。第二我觉得我们其实比外部说的更强 believe 这个。所以它真那么 key 内部怎么想有时我们 reword statement 因为 like 大家可能觉得我们太 over the top 但内部我们那样想、我们 put 出的是更软版本有时。(01:34:28)：然后第三是 Ben 说的我们想很多 drive the race to the top。就如果你不在 game 喊……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I could talk to you forever, Amol, but two more questions just to round out the conversation and touch on some stuff that I've hinted at a number of times. One is I want to take us actually to failure corner because someone listening to this may be like, "All right, look at this guy just worked at all these amazing companies, cold email, the CPO at Anthropic, got a job, joined this rocket ship. It's all been up and to the right, just killing it constantly." What's a story from your career where things didn't work out when you failed and what did you learn from that experience?
turns.zh: 我能永远聊 Amol 但还有两个问题 round out 对话和 touch 我暗示多次的东西。一是我要带我们到 failure corner 因为有人听这个可能 like 看这人 work 过所有这些 amazing 公司、冷邮件 Anthropic CPO、得工作、join 这个火箭。一直往上右、一直 killing。你职业有没有事不 work、你 fail、学到什么的故事？

turns.speaker: Amol Avasare
turns.en: I have a couple. I think it's very much not that way. I feel like it was a lot of squiggly lines to get here. The biggest I'd say is just founding a company, raising a bunch of money, having employees, and then having to shut it down and tell your investors that you've lost the money and that you had a vision of what you're going to do and that it's not going to happen. And so that I think is probably the biggest one. We spent three years on it. It was not like a, "Oh, we tried something part-time." It was like, "No, we went for it." We had spent three years, raised a couple of mil. We had maybe seven, 10 employees at our biggest. And it was something that we really believed in. It was around mental health and how you can quantify mental health to help understand or get early predictors of things like generalized anxiety, major depression. So it's stuff that we really, really believed in. (01:36:39): But ultimately, in our early 20s, we had no idea what we're doing at the time and many things I do differently, but that was just a very, very, very painful process. I think the good thing was we kept our investors in the loop the whole time, so 20 founders who are struggling out there. Send those monthly investor updates. It's really easy to send those when things are great. It's really hard to send those when things are bad. You just bat it down. You sit down and send an update to your investors about why everything you talked about last month did not go to plan, but it's just the right thing to do, and it keeps people in the loop, and it avoids surprises. But it's still so tough when you're then calling up the investors to be like, "Hey, we're shutting down or making that decision," everyone who believed in you and it becomes such a big part of the identity. It's very, very tough. (01:37:29): So man, that was just brutal. It's brutal. And it took me, I think, a number of years to truly get over. I think that it's a tough thing, but you get so much from that experience that it's hard to see in the moment. And I think without doing that, I would not have gone into this. I was not a PM before. I didn't have any of these skills. I'd never worked on products. I didn't know how to cold email really. And so it was through that job that I learned a ton of the skills that made this career path viable for me. And it's just really hard to see that in the moment when you're looking at a point in time. It's much easier to draw the line looking back. (01:38:07): But I think that'd be my takeaway is just keep in mind that it's a long game and some of those things... I'm so grateful for that experience now. I'm so grateful that it failed and went that way, actually. It's very painful because it wouldn't have led to what I'm doing now. And so it's a tough thing, but the positives can come from it.
turns.zh: 我有几个。我觉得非常不是那样。我觉得很多 squiggly line 到这。最大我会说是 founding 公司、raise 了一堆钱、有员工、然后得 shut down、告诉投资人你 lost 钱和你有 vision 要做什么、不会发生。那个我觉得是最大。我们花了三年。不是哦 part-time 试。是真 go。三年、raise 了几百万。最大时大概 7 到 10 员工。是我们真相信的。关于心理健康、怎么量化心理健康帮理解或得早期预测广泛性焦虑、重度抑郁。所以我们真真相信。(01:36:39)：但最终我们二十出头时不知道做什么、很多我会不同做但那是真真真痛苦过程。好在我们一直 keep 投资人 in loop，所以 20 个 founder 挣扎中的。发那些月度投资人 update。事好时容易发。事坏时难发。你 bat down、坐下发 update 给投资人关于为什么你上个月说的一切没按计划，但就是对的事、keep 人 in loop、避免 surprise。但仍那么 tough 当你 then 打电话给投资人 like hey 我们 shut down 或做那个决定、每个相信你的人、变成 identity 大部分。非常 tough。(01:37:29)：所以天哪那 brutal。brutal。我花了好几年真 get over。我觉得 tough 事但你从那个经验得那么多……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What I love about this is a lot of people have these times in their career where they're like, "It's all over. I failed in such a big way and my reputation's screwed and people were counting on me and now they see I'm an imposter. I never knew what I was doing. And after all, now they finally see." And just seeing that, and this was three years, I'm looking at your LinkedIn, you had seven employees, something like that, and then it's like masterclass, Mercury, Anthropic. I think it's inspiring to hear a story like that to know that you can have a big failure like that and things can work out. That is not the end. Okay. So at 2023, I was going to go on pat leave because my wife's pregnant and I was just like, "Wait, what do I do with the newsletter? I need to take some time off. That would be really nice to take a month or two off." (01:39:13): And so my plan was, "Okay, I'm going to do a bunch of guest posts where people line up." I put out a call for guest posts, people apply, I pick a few and then I kind of slot them in ahead of time so I could take time off. So I put out this call, "Hey, who wants to write a guest post for my newsletter?" I got 500 plus applications. One of those applications was from you and the pitch was essentially how a traumatic brain injury made me a better product manager. And I still remember reading the first draft you sent me and I was just like, "Holy shit, this story is incredible." It's just like you feel such feelings and it was just so tactically interesting and useful like, "Oh wow, this is actually going to make me a better product manager." Share the story of the brain injury that you went through and just the journey that you went on there because this is going to blow people's minds.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个是很多人职业有这种时候就完了。我大 fail、reputation 糟、人指望我、现在看到我是 imposter、我从不知道在做什么、现在终于看到。看那个、这是三年、我看你 LinkedIn 你有七员工什么的、然后 masterclass、Mercury、Anthropic。我觉得 inspire 听这种故事知道你能有大 fail、事能 work out。那不是结束。好。2023 年我要 pat leave 因为我老婆怀孕我就好我拿 newsletter 怎么办？我需要 take time off。一两个月 off 会很好。(01:39:13)：所以我计划好我做一堆客座文章、人排队。我发 call for 客座文章、人 apply、我挑几个 slot ahead 这样我能 take time off。我发这个 call 嘿谁想为我 newsletter 写客座文章？我收到 500+ 申请。其中一个是你、pitch 基本是 how a traumatic brain injury made me a better PM。我还记得读你发我的第一稿就天哪这个故事 incredible。就你感受那么多感情、那么战术有趣有用 like 哦哇这真会让我变更好 PM。分享你脑损伤的故事和旅程因为这会 blow 人 mind。

turns.speaker: Amol Avasare
turns.en: It was the toughest time in my life. It made shutting down a company being like, "Oh, that was nothing actually." Just funny how perspective works that way. Back in early 2022, I had a traumatic brain injury. So I'd done MMA for many years. I'd done Muay Thai, which is a type of martial arts for many years, never had a problem. And it's just one of the things that happens, the wrong session. It's just a normal day of sparring, nothing crazy. You get the wrong hit to the head in the wrong way, and my whole life changed. And basically I spent nine months. I was off work for nine months. The first couple of months were brutal. It took me roughly half a year till I was comfortable walking again. It was very, very difficult. The first two, three months beyond just showering and going to the bathroom, my wife did everything for me, including texting my friends. (01:40:59): I would listen to music for maybe 20 seconds and feel like I needed to vomit. I couldn't look at screens at all. And it was a very, very long recovery. It was not clear to me that I would ever work again for a while actually. And it was like we'd even discussed my wife, what would we do in that case, et cetera. And we had to think even on those levels. And through a lot of pushing and really working through myself, and you have to just slowly increase your tolerance to things. It's a brutal process, but you need to slowly expose yourself to different things and just get better and better at each little thing, actively work on that, don't push it too far, otherwise you have a big setback. It basically got to the point then where over nine months and then that it returned to work and then it slowly got better. And the part, Lenny, you don't know is in mid-2023, we posted that newsletter and a month later I got re-injured actually.
turns.zh: 那是我人生最 tough 时间。它让 shut down 公司像哦那其实 nothing。有趣 perspective 那样 work。2022 年初我有创伤性脑损伤。我做了很多年 MMA。泰拳多年从没问题。就是发生的事、wrong session。就正常 sparring 日、没什么 crazy。你以错的方式被 wrong hit 到头、我整个人生变了。基本我花 9 个月。我 9 个月没工作。前几个月 brutal。大概半年我才 comfortable 走路。非常非常难。前两三个月除了洗澡和上厕所我老婆为我做一切、包括给我朋友发短信。(01:40:59)：我听音乐 20 秒就觉得要吐。完全不能看屏幕。非常非常长恢复。有段时间我不 clear 我会再 work。我们甚至讨论我老婆如果那个 case 怎么办等等。我们得 even 在那些 level 想。通过很多 pushing 和真 work through 自己、你得慢慢增加对东西的容忍。brutal 过程但你需要慢慢暴露自己于不同东西、每个小事变更好、actively work 那个、不 push 太远否则大 setback。基本到 then 9 个月 then 回 work 然后慢慢变好。Lenny 你不知道的是 2023 年中我们 post 那个 newsletter 一个月后我 re-injured。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, wow.
turns.zh: 哦哇。

turns.speaker: Amol Avasare
turns.en: And when you have a brain injury, until you're 100% healed, your risk of another concussion or a brain injury is elevated. When you're 100% healed, your risk falls down to that of a non-concussed population. But until that time, and even if you're like 95% healed, you're not 100% healed. And it was just an innocuous sort of in everyday life getting off a plane, a bag sort of hit me on the head type thing. And I was off work for two months when I... One month into joining Mercury, one month in, I'm like, "Sorry guys, I need to peace out for three months." And then it was a very, very long recovery from that. And I'm actually still not 100% healed. So I'm mostly good, but I have times when I have dizziness and headaches and other things that I need to work around. Overall, I feel like it's one of the best things that could have happened to me, and I think that keeping that mindset helps. (01:42:51): And there's a point when you can take that too far when that view is detached from reality, but I think it's just made me so much better and more effective as a person. A lot of the same habits, I don't drink alcohol, I don't drink caffeine, I have to do a bunch of these things for my physical health. I just have to do them. So I keep doing them. I take breaks. This is a really big one. You might think even in a place like Anthropic, how do you survive in this way? It's like even on the craziest days, Lenny, between the start of the day and lunch and between lunch and the end of the day, I take a short break. Even on the craziest days with model launches, et cetera, I'm lucky we have a meditation area in the office that I'll go to. (01:43:29): And then the whole side of things around meditation that I talked about in that post, I think both you and I have done a retreat at Spirit Rock and doing a meditation retreat changed my life. And it's something that I do at least once a year now. I have one coming up relatively soon as well. And just I think all of that has helped with better managing the physical side of it because this job is very taxing, and then emotionally having a little bit of space to what happens. So you have sort of awareness on one side, you have the reality on the other side. And reality's crazy here, man. Reality's insane. There's so much happening every day. There's so much noise, it's mind-blowing. And so that relationship between awareness and reality, that's where you have choice that you sort of learn from deep meditation on how to shift that and apply your choice there. (01:44:26): I think that that is the thing that has helped me significantly with just keeping a more level head. I think a lot of staying in this game in this level of intensity is just keep your head, just don't lose your head in the crazy times. And I think all of that that I've gone through has helped me do this without resorting to unhealthy coping mechanisms.
turns.zh: 当你有脑损伤、直到 100% healed 你另一个 concussion 或脑损伤风险 elevated。当你 100% healed 风险降到 non-concussed 人群。但直到那个时间即使你 95% healed 不是 100%。就是 innocuous sort 日常下飞机包 hit 我头那种。我 2 个月没工作当我……加入 Mercury 一个月、一个月就对不起大家我需要 peace out 三个月。然后非常非常长恢复。我其实仍没 100% healed。所以大多好但我有晕和头痛等时候我得 work around。总的来说我觉得它是能发生在我身上的最好事之一、我觉得 keep 那个 mindset 有帮助。(01:42:51)：有 point 你能 take 太远当那个 view 脱离现实但我觉得它让我作为人变得更好更有效。很多同样习惯、我不喝酒、不喝咖啡因、我得做 bunch 这些 for 身体健康。我就得做。所以 keep 做。我 take break。这个真大。你可能觉得即使在 Anthropic 这种地方你怎么 survive 这样。就最 crazy 日 Lenny 在一天开始和午饭之间、午饭和一天结束之间我 take short break。即使最 crazy 日 model launch 等我们 lucky 办公有冥想区我去。(01:43:29)：然后冥想那边我在那 post 谈的、我觉得你我都在 Spirit Rock 做过 retreat、做冥想 retreat 改变我人生。是我现在至少每年一次做的事。我有一个 relatively soon 来。就是我觉得所有那个帮 with……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. Amol, you're such an inspiration in so many ways. There's so many reasons that you would not have been successful and things would not have worked out. And there's so many lessons to learn from just the stories you've shared in the journey you've been on to help people overcome challenges they're having. If you can come back from an insane... Was it like a kick to the head? Is that what happened?
turns.zh: 哇。Amol 你在那么多方面是 inspiration。有那么多理由你不会成功、事不会 work out。有那么多 lesson 从你分享的故事和旅程帮人克服他们挑战。如果你能从 insane……是 kick 到头吗？那是发生什么？

turns.speaker: Amol Avasare
turns.en: It was a kick to the head. That's correct. Yes.
turns.zh: 是 kick 到头。对。是。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just feeling like you may not be able to listen to music to just leading growth at the fastest growing company in history. There's also just a lesson here of constraints. Again, you mentioned this idea of just the power of constraints. You're forced to take breaks, you're forced to go meditate in a way that's really helpful and it's a lesson for us all. This is actually really good for us all.
turns.zh: 就感觉你可能没法听音乐到 leading 增长历史上增长最快公司。也有 constraint 的 lesson。你提到 constraint 的力量。你被迫 take break、被迫冥想、真有帮助、对我们都是 lesson。这其实对我们都很好。

turns.speaker: Amol Avasare
turns.en: Yeah. I think that freedom through constraints is one of the big takeaways I've had during that time. Because if you have these constraints, you're forced to adapt and it creates, gives you in a business setting, you have to focus more in a personal setting. And if the constraint is, "I can't do anything and I'm injured. I don't know what's going to happen. I don't know. I'm going to get better," you have two choices. You're like, one, are you just going to resist and fight with reality and really suffer from that, or are you going to accept the situation and not let that affect you emotionally? And it's not to say I did everything, man. I was like, every single thing I could do, diet, I was like, "I'm on it. Every action I can take, I'm on it." (01:46:16): But then you have a choice of, are you going to let the impact of that define your happiness or not? And I think that that's the thing when the impacts maybe are not coming, you have to then adapt to, "Okay, what do I want my happiness to be?" And one of the meditation teachers said that true freedom in life is learning how to be content when you don't get what you want. And it's not to say you shouldn't do something when you don't get what you want, but I think that that takeaway of just can you be content and not have your happiness rely on getting something. It's a challenge. I'm not perfect at it, but I think it's probably one of the biggest takeaways from that whole thing.
turns.zh: 对。我觉得通过 constraint 的自由是那段时间我的大 takeaway 之一。因为如果你有这些 constraint 你被迫 adapt、创造、在 business setting 你得更聚焦、在 personal setting。如果 constraint 是我没法做任何事、我 injured、我不知道会怎样、我不知道我会好，你有两选择。一是你就 resist 和 fight reality、真 suffer，或你接受情况、不让它 emotional 影响你。不是说全做了 man。我 like 每件能做的事、diet 我 like 我在 it。每个能 take 的 action 我在 it。(01:46:16)：但你 then 有选择你让那个影响定义你 happiness 吗？我觉得那个是当影响可能不来你 then adapt 好我要我 happiness 是什么？一个冥想老师说 true freedom in life 是学习你没得到你要的时候怎么 content。不是说你不该做什么当你没得到你要的但我觉得那个 takeaway 就你能 content、不让 happiness rely on 得到什么。是 challenge。我不 perfect 但我觉得大概是那个 whole thing 最大 takeaway 之一。

turns.en: Incredible. And we'll link to the post of folks who want to read this. Before we get to a very exciting lightning round, is there anything else you wanted to share, or should we just jump right in?
turns.zh: incredible。我们会链接到 post 给想读的。before 闪电问答还有什么想分享、还是就 jump？

turns.speaker: Amol Avasare
turns.en: I think we can jump into it.

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, we covered a lot of ground. Okay, here we go. I've got five questions for you. First question, what are two or three books you recommend most to other people?
turns.zh: 哦我们覆盖了很多。好来。我有五个问题。第一个问题，你最常推荐给人的两三本书？

turns.speaker: Amol Avasare
turns.en: It probably ties to a lot of what I just talked about. I think a lot about meditation and my emotional state. What I spend most of my time thinking and reading and researching and working on outside of work. So my recommendations very related to that. The first is a book called Joy of Living by a Buddhist monk. His name's Yongey Mingyur Rinpoche. It's just really about how you can start to think about your life experience in a different way and have tactics of what to do to kind of change just how you think about things. This is one where I've recommended to people. (01:47:49): Yeah, I've recommended to a lot of people and they've really, really enjoyed it. I think another one is Awareness by Anthony de Mello, which is a kind of similar thing but from a different angle. Those two I consistently recommend to people. And then the third one is more relevant to product in many ways is Thinking In Bets by Annie Duke. I think just being able to break down a situation when someone's like, "I don't know, it'll get done in time. Okay. Can you put a number to that? What percentage or likelihood is it?" Those types of things, I think, are just so tactically helpful in product.
turns.zh: 大概 tie 到我刚聊的。我想很多冥想和我情绪状态。我工作外花最多时间想、读、研究、work 的。所以我推荐很相关。第一是一本叫 Joy of Living 的书、一个佛教僧侣写的。他叫 Yongey Mingyur Rinpoche。就是关于怎么开始不同想你的生活体验、有 tactics 做什么 kind 改变怎么想东西。这是推荐给人的。(01:47:49)：对推荐给很多人他们真真喜欢。我觉得另一本是 Anthony de Mello 的 Awareness，类似但从不同角度。那两本我持续推荐。第三更相关产品很多是 Annie Duke 的 Thinking In Bets。我觉得能拆解情况当有人 like 我不知道能按时完成。好你能给数字吗？什么百分比或可能性？那些我觉得就战术 helpful 在产品。

turns.en: Favorite recent movie or TV show?
turns.zh: 最近最喜欢的电影或剧集？

turns.zh: 电影大概 Marty Supreme。是我最近看的少数之一。我觉得 great。觉得 insane。绝对 insane 电影。ridiculous 但我爱。TV 我一阵没看 TV。大概奥运会如果那算。

turns.en: Is there a product that you love just like, I don't know, when you discovered recently or just one you have in your life that's like, "Oh, this is very cool. People might want to know about it"?
turns.zh: 有产品你爱就像最近发现或生活中有的 like 哦这很 cool 大家可能想知道？

turns.speaker: Amol Avasare
turns.en: Yeah. So this is a funny one. I was in Japan last week and I was sleeping in this hotel and I just really loved the pillow that I had in this hotel. It was very random. I just at times had neck and upper trap pain and sometimes I've been frustrated with my pillow because I sometimes sleep facing up, sometimes sideways and the height's not quite right. And I was just like, "This pillow is just great." And basically this pillow is full of beads. And so you can naturally shift the height of the pillow while you're sleeping even unconsciously without thinking. And so I looked at the tag. I was like, "What is this?" I ordered it to [inaudible 01:49:26] Amazon Japan, and I bought it back with me on the plane. And so I have the name here. It's called the Maruhachi Shinsui Maruhatchi Pro pillow, and you can only get it in Japan, but they're shipped to the US, no affiliation. And I think that has changed my life in the last week.
turns.zh: 对。这个 funny。我上周在日本、睡这个酒店我真爱那个枕头。很 random。我有时有颈和上 trap 痛、有时我 frustrated 枕头因为我有时面朝上睡、有时侧睡高度不太对。我就这枕头 great。基本这个枕头满 beads。所以你能自然 shift 枕头高度当你睡甚至无意识不想。我看 tag like 这是什么？我在 Amazon Japan 订、带上飞机。名字这里。叫 Maruhachi Shinsui Maruhatchi Pro 枕头、只能日本得但他们 ship 到美国、无 affiliation。我觉得上周改变了我人生。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is an awesome pick. Do you have a favorite life motto that you often come back to in work or in life?
turns.zh: 那是 awesome pick。有最常回到的、在 work 或生活有用的人生格言？

turns.speaker: Amol Avasare
turns.en: Main one I'd say is just she'll be right. This is a very common Aussie saying. It's like she will be right. She'll be right. It's a common Aussie saying when we're faced with a tough or difficult situation, you're kind of dismissing the severity of it in a way by saying like, "Eh, it'll be fine." And I think that that's just such a good metaphor. It's such a good tactic in many, many cases. And then I think the other one is just sometimes in life, you just have to go for it. And that is something that this guy, Eros Resmini, who is the CMO of Discord, who is a very close advisor to me as a founder, he would push me on this and that was something that he would often say is just like, "Just go for it." And I think that it's a very helpful thing of you can sit there thinking, "Should I do this, should I not?" And sometimes in life, you just have to go for it.
turns.zh: 主要我会说就 she'll be right。这是很常见澳洲说法。就是 she will be right。she'll be right。当我们面对 tough 或难情况时常见澳洲说法、你 kind of dismiss 严重性像 eh 会 fine。我觉得那是那么好 metaphor。那么多 case 那么好 tactic。然后另一个是有时人生你就得 go for it。那是这个 guy Eros Resmini——Discord CMO——我作为创始人时很近 advisor、他 push 我这个、他常说就 go for it。我觉得很有帮助。你能坐那想我该做这个吗、我不该吗？有时人生你就得 go for it。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love the combo of those two. Just sometimes just go for it and she'll be right. So good. Okay. Final question. Okay. So I'm curious, used to be into martial arts, that didn't go great. Do you have a new hobby that you find yourself loving? Do you make time for hobbies?
turns.zh: 我爱那两个 combo。就有时 go for it 和 she'll be right。太好。好。最后一个问题。好奇你以前武术、那个不太好。你有新爱好你发现自己爱吗？你 make 时间给爱好吗？

turns.speaker: Amol Avasare
turns.en: I think I'm just quite tight on time for hobbies. I would say I think it's largely just work and have my body function and then take care of the most important relationships around me. I think maybe the one hobby I'd say is just I'm really into sports and I've gotten more into sports at football in particular.
turns.zh: 我觉得我挺紧时间给爱好。我会说大概就是 work 和让身体 function 然后 take care 最重要的关系。也许一个爱好我会说我真 into 体育、我更 into 体育 football 特别。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Like watching.
turns.zh: 看。

turns.en: Watching. Certainly not playing. My wife's from Michigan and she took me to a game at the Big House and it just changed my life. From then on, I was like, I'm a Wolverines fan and big Wolverines fan, big 49ers fan. I just love football. So that's probably the one that comes to mind.
turns.zh: 看。definitely 不是踢。我老婆从 Michigan、她带我去 Big House 看比赛、改变我人生。从 then 我就我是 Wolverines fan、大 Wolverines fan、大 49ers fan。我就爱 football。所以那个大概 come to mind。
